html:
The Fair Labor Standards Act was a United States law, signed on 25 June 1938, that set the first national minimum wage, a limit on the working week and a ban on most child labour.

It was one of the last big laws of the New Deal. President Franklin D. Roosevelt wanted to lift pay and spread work around during the Great Depression. An earlier try, the codes of the National Industrial Recovery Act, had been struck down by the Supreme Court in 1935.

The act set a minimum wage of 25 cents an hour and a standard week of 44 hours, falling to 40 hours by 1940. Hours beyond that had to be paid at time and a half. That overtime rule made the five-day, 40-hour week the norm, and so helped fix the two-day weekend in American life.

Many workers were left out, notably farm and domestic workers, who were mostly Black in the South. The Supreme Court upheld the act in 1941. It is the base of American wage and hour law today, and the long push for shorter hours it completed goes back to the eight-hour day movement.
sum: The Fair Labor Standards Act was a United States law, signed on 25 June 1938, that set the first national minimum wage, a limit on the working week and a ban on most child labour.
